Hallowed

/HAL-ohd/ - the stress falls on HAL · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Hallowed means revered, consecrated.

To the divers, the old wreck is hallowed water — no souvenirs, no shouting, no hands on the rail.

Worked Example

The family's hallowed sourdough starter — begun by a great-aunt nobody living ever met — rides to every reunion buckled into its own seat, and nobody laughs at that anymore.

Hallowed means treated as holy, whether or not a religion is anywhere in sight: hallowed ground, hallowed halls, hallowed traditions. The tell is behavior — voices drop, hats come off, jokes wait outside. Old and famous are facts about a thing; hallowed is what people do around it.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

sacred: Sacred means formally set apart as holy — the word a faith itself would use for its altars, relics, and rites. Hallowed climbs to the same height by a slower road: a thing becomes hallowed because generations treat it with reverence. A chapel is sacred by consecration; a battlefield grows hallowed by remembrance.

holy: Holy means belonging to the divine — gods, scripture, heaven's own things. Hallowed is holiness conferred by reverence: bared heads and lowered voices can make a courtroom hallowed with no religion in sight. Holy points at heaven; hallowed points at how people behave.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

everyday: ordinary, nothing set apart

commonplace: so usual no one lowers their voice for it

Where it sits · how much awe surrounds it — respected → cherished → hallowed

respected vs. hallowed: Respected earns a nod, and it is far milder than hallowed — nobody whispers around a respected parking rule.

cherished vs. hallowed: Cherished is loved and protected, but hallowed is stronger still — cherished things are held close; hallowed things are approached quietly.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — hallow

Root — hallow: to make holy; a holy one, a saint (Old English hālgian)

Suffix — -ed

Suffix — -ed: adjective ending: made so

Put it together

Put it together: Hallow (to make holy) + -ed = made holy. Old English hālgian did the church's heavy lifting for centuries, and it left one spectacular fingerprint on the calendar: Halloween is 'All Hallows' Eve,' the night before All Hallows' Day — the feast of all the saints.

Use the root in a new word: Halloween

Use the root in a new word: Halloween: By six o'clock on Halloween, the porch bowl was down to the candy nobody wants.

Word Choice

formal / reverent

Hallowed marks what people treat as sacred — ground, halls, names, rules. It is stronger than respected and warmer than official words like consecrated. Its unit-neighbor venerate (in the reference list) is the verb for the act; hallowed describes what long veneration leaves behind. And spell with care: hallowed, not hollowed — one letter separates the sacred from the empty.
